title: Ask a little more
description: Use who, what, and where in everyday questions.

sections.title: Choose a question word
sections.body: Use who for a person, what for a thing, and where for a place. 'Who is your teacher?' 'What is in your backpack?' 'Where is the classroom?'

sections.title: Keep the question in order
sections.body: With be, put the verb before the subject. 'Where is the kitchen?' With other present-simple verbs, use do or does. 'What do you read?' Ask a partner three questions and listen to each answer.

question: Choose the question that asks about a place.
explanation: Where asks about a place, and a garden is a place.

title: Ordering a meal
description: Ask for food and drinks politely.

sections.title: Make a simple request
sections.body: Say 'I would like' when ordering. 'I would like some bread, please.' Use 'Can I have' for a friendly request. 'Can I have some water, please?'

sections.title: Check and finish
sections.body: Ask 'How much is it?' when you need the price. Say 'Thank you' when the food arrives. Practise with a partner. One person is hungry and orders breakfast. The other takes the order. Then switch.

question: Which request sounds polite?
options: Can I have some water, please?
explanation: Can I have and please make this a polite request.

title: Yesterday in a few words
description: Describe a finished day using the past simple.

sections.title: Talk about a finished action
sections.body: Use the past simple for an action completed at a known past time. 'We visited our neighbour yesterday.' Regular verbs usually add -ed. Irregular verbs change. Go becomes went. 'I went to the festival on Saturday.'

sections.title: Ask about yesterday
sections.body: Use did and the base verb. 'Did you enjoy the festival?' For a negative, use did not. 'We did not stay late.' Tell a partner about yesterday using three finished actions.

question: Choose the correct past-simple question.
explanation: After did, use the base verb visit rather than visited.

title: Plans for the weekend
description: Talk about intentions with going to.

sections.title: Say what you intend to do
sections.body: Use am, is, or are with going to and the base verb. 'I am going to invite a friend.' 'We are going to prepare lunch.' These are plans you have already thought about.

sections.title: Ask and respond
sections.body: Ask 'What are you going to do tomorrow?' Add a time or a place to your answer. 'I am going to repair my bicycle in the garden.' Share one plan with a partner and ask a follow-up question.

question: Which sentence describes a future intention?
options: We are going to prepare lunch tomorrow.
explanation: Going to describes the intention, and tomorrow makes the future time clear.

title: Make your ideas flow
description: Connect a reason, a result, and a contrast.

sections.title: Choose the right connection
sections.body: Although introduces a contrast within a sentence. 'Although the task was a challenge, we found a solution.' However introduces a contrasting sentence. 'The plan was ambitious. However, our group had enough time.' As a result introduces a consequence. 'We practised daily. As a result, we felt more confident.'

sections.title: Build a short paragraph
sections.body: Write three sentences about learning a language. Explain one reason, one result, and one contrast. Check that each linking phrase matches the relationship between your ideas. Read the paragraph aloud.

question: Which phrase correctly completes the second sentence? We practised daily. _____, we felt more confident.
explanation: Feeling more confident is a consequence of daily practice, so as a result fits the relationship.

title: A clear request
description: Write a short message that is easy to answer.

sections.title: Give just enough context
sections.body: Start with why you are writing. 'I am organising our reading group.' Then make one clear request. 'Could you suggest a book for independent learners?' Include a useful date if you need a reply by a particular time.

sections.title: Read it as the recipient
sections.body: Check that the reader can tell what you want and when you need it. Finish politely. 'Thank you for your help.' Write a message asking about an opportunity to volunteer. Remove any details the reader does not need.

question: Which request is easiest to answer?
options: I have many questions about our group.
Could you suggest one book for our reading group by Friday?
explanation: The request specifies one action, the purpose, and a useful reply date.

title: An argument with support
description: Connect a claim to evidence and an explanation.

sections.title: Find the parts
sections.body: A claim states an idea. Evidence supports it. An explanation shows why that evidence matters. 'The library should open later' is a claim. A record of evening visits could provide evidence. An explanation could be 'Many visits happen after 6 p.m., so evening opening would suit students who work or study late.'

sections.title: Test the connection
sections.body: Ask whether the evidence actually supports the claim. A personal preference is not enough to show what everyone needs. Look for an assumption between the evidence and the conclusion. Discuss what extra information would make the argument more convincing.

question: Which detail best supports a claim that students need later library hours?
options: A survey shows many students cannot visit before closing time.
explanation: The survey connects students' availability directly to the proposed opening hours.

title: Leave room for uncertainty
description: Use cautious language when evidence is limited.

sections.title: Match confidence to evidence
sections.body: Words such as may, appears, and suggests help you avoid claiming more than you know. 'The new timetable may improve attendance.' 'These results suggest that shorter sessions help.' Cautious wording makes the degree of certainty clear.

sections.title: Keep the useful detail
sections.body: Caution should not make your message vague. Say what happened and what remains uncertain. 'Attendance rose this month, but we need more evidence before drawing a conclusion.' Practise describing a small classroom survey without assuming it represents everyone.

question: Which sentence best matches limited evidence from one small class?
options: Every student learns faster in the morning.
The results prove that mornings are always better.
The results suggest that this class may benefit from morning sessions.
explanation: Suggest and may reflect the limited evidence, and this class keeps the claim appropriately narrow.

title: Choose the right register
description: Adapt your wording to the audience and purpose.

sections.title: What register means
sections.body: Register is the level and style of language suited to a situation. 'Can you explain that?' works in a friendly conversation. 'Could you elaborate on that point?' fits a formal discussion. Both can be clear and respectful.

sections.title: Change style without changing meaning
sections.body: Rewrite a request for a classmate and then for an unfamiliar organisation. Keep the core request clear. Adjust the greeting, word choice, and closing. Formal language should still be coherent and concise, rather than unnecessarily elaborate.

question: Which request best suits a formal discussion?
options: Could you clarify the reasoning behind your proposal?
Can you tell me a bit more about your idea?
What is up with your idea?
explanation: The wording is precise and polite, using a formal register. The second option is polite but more conversational.

title: Read a claim closely
description: Separate a plausible claim from a justified conclusion.

sections.title: Look beneath the wording
sections.body: A compelling sentence can still rest on weak evidence. Identify its claim, source, and assumptions. Notice words such as all, never, and unprecedented. Ask what would be needed to justify them and whether an alternative explanation is plausible.

sections.title: Compare explanations
sections.body: When two reports disagree, examine the discrepancy before choosing one. They may measure different groups or time periods. Write a tentative conclusion that acknowledges the available evidence. Keep any uncertainty explicit rather than hiding it behind confident wording.

question: Two reports reach different conclusions about the same programme. What should you check first?
options: Which report has the more dramatic headline.
Whether they studied comparable groups, periods, and measures.
Which conclusion you already agree with.
explanation: Differences in groups, periods, or measures can explain a discrepancy and affect whether the conclusions can be compared.
